query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy multilayer protective coatings, the engineered multilayer interfaces serve as dislocation barriers that create localized gradients in the activation energy for plastic flow. This synergistic effect delays dislocation nucleation and motion, resulting in enhanced resistance to time-dependent (creep) plastic deformation compared to homogeneous HEA coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited high-entropy alloy coatings with engineered microstructures featuring finely controlled, multilayer interfaces and inherent lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Systematically fabricate coatings with varying multilayer interface spacings and chemistries and compare their creep response to that of homogeneous HEA coatings made under identical conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature and sustained stress conditions typical of protective coating service (e.g., temperatures in the 500–600 °C range under constant loading conditions) where creep is prominent.
generation.structural_mediator: The multilayer interfaces acting as physical barriers to dislocation motion, thereby locally increasing the activation energy required for creep-related plastic flow.
generation.mechanism: Interfaces impede dislocation nucleation and slow the movement of dislocations by imposing barriers, which elevates the effective activation energy for plastic deformation. This results in a lower creep rate compared to coatings without such engineered interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayer coatings will exhibit significantly lower creep rates and reduced dislocation activity in the vicinity of interfaces relative to homogeneous coatings. A systematic variation in interface spacing/chemistry should correlate with changes in creep resistance, revealing an optimum configuration for maximum creep resistance.
generation.baseline: Homogeneous HEA coatings without engineered multilayer interfaces are expected to show higher creep rates and more extensive dislocation activity under the same test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant under moderate to high temperatures (approximately 500–600 °C) and relevant stress levels where dislocation-mediated creep prevails. At temperatures or stress conditions where diffusion mechanisms dominate, the effect may be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of creep rate reduction and the quantitative dependence on interface spacing/chemistry remain uncertain and may vary with subtle microstructural differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: (1) multilayer HEA coatings with systematically varied interface spacing and chemistry and (2) homogeneous HEA coatings without engineered interfaces. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature creep testing (e.g., at 500–600 °C under constant applied stress) while monitoring in situ creep responses and dislocation dynamics using nanoindentation and high-resolution microscopy (SEM/TEM).
measurements: Activation energy estimations from creep curves
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If multilayer coatings do not consistently exhibit lower creep rates and reduced dislocation activity compared to homogeneous coatings or if variations in interface spacing/chemistry do not correlate with measurable changes in creep resistance, then the hypothesis that engineered interfaces mediate enhanced creep resistance by acting as dislocation barriers is falsified.

To enhance the operational damage resistance of hydraulic machinery, this study employed laser cladding technology to fabricate a Co37.4Cr30Ni20Al5Ti5Nb2.6 high-entropy alloy coating on 04Cr13Ni5Mo substrate. The influence of laser power on the microstructure and properties of the coating was systematically investigated. Based on preliminary research, the friction-wear performance and cavitation erosion behavior of the coatings prepared at 3000 W, 3200 W, and 3400 W were specifically examined. Results indicate that as the laser power increased from 3000 W to 3400 W, the microhardness of the coating gradually decreased from 345.3 HV0.2. At 3000 W, the precipitation of trace strengthening phases significantly enhanced the mechanical properties. In wear tests under a 20 N load for 30 min, the wear rate of the coating prepared at 3000 W was 1.41 × 10−4 mm3/(N·m), which is 13.5% lower than that of the 3200 W coating (1.63 × 10−4 mm3/(N·m)) and 16.07% higher in wear resistance compared to the substrate. Cavitation erosion tests revealed that after 20 h of ultrasonic vibration, the mass loss of the 3000 W coating was only 2.35 mg, representing an 88.89% reduction compared to the substrate

High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.

The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol−1, whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol−1. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. AbstractThere is a strong demand for materials with inherently high creep resistance in the harsh environment of next-generation nuclear reactors. High entropy alloys have drawn intense attention in this regard due to their excellent elevated temperature properties and irradiation resistance. Here, the time-dependent plastic deformation behavior of two refractory high entropy alloys was investigated, namely HfTaTiVZr and TaTiVWZr. These alloys are based on reduced activity metals from the 4-5-6 elemental palette that would allow easy post-service recycling after use in nuclear reactors. The creep behavior was investigated using nano-indentation over the temperature range of 298 K to 573 K under static and dynamic loads up to 5 N. Creep stress exponent for HfTaTiVZr and TaTiVWZr was found to be in the range of 20–140 and the activation volume was ~16–20b3, indicating dislocation dominated mechanism. The stress exponent increased with increasing indentation depth due to a higher density of dislocations and their entanglement at larger depth and the exponent decreased with increasing temperature due to thermally activated dislocations. frame.goal: To understand and quantitatively demonstrate the mechanism by which these coatings resist time-dependent (creep) plastic deformation under service conditions.
frame.limitation: The fundamental mechanistic origins for the exceptional resistance to creep deformation in HEA multilayers remain unexplained, particularly the role of the multilayer interfaces and compositional complexity.

decision.trend: Early HEA studies focused on bulk creep behavior, demonstrating that mechanisms such as low stacking‐fault energy, high lattice stability, and intrinsic resistance to dislocation motion are key to achieving low creep rates. Later, simulation work has dissected how stress, temperature, and lattice misfit affect creep by modulating dislocation nucleation and motion. However, while these studies have clarified how intrinsic lattice factors govern creep in homogeneous HEAs or superalloys, they have not addressed how engineered multilayer interfaces—with their controlled spacing and compositional gradients—might further impede time‐dependent plastic flow.
decision.unsolved: The role of designed multilayer interfaces in blocking dislocation motion and creating a gradient in activation energy for plastic flow remains untested. In particular, a controlled comparative study directly contrasting multilayer HEA coatings with homogeneous HEA coatings under similar creep conditions is lacking, leaving the actual mechanism by which the interfaces enhance creep resistance unresolved.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the multilayer interface spacing and chemistry by fabricating multilayer versus homogeneous HEA coatings under identical thermal-stress conditions, then measuring and comparing their creep rates and dislocation activities using in situ nanoindentation and high-temperature mechanical testing
decision.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that engineered multilayer interfaces enhance creep resistance by serving as dislocation barriers, creating gradients in activation energy for plastic flow. It builds on past insights from bulk HEA and simulation studies, and the controlled comparison is precisely tuned to isolate the influence of the interface—which is the key unsolved aspect identified in earlier research.
